c.tagline: A pastel-walled colonial port on the Gulf, ramparts and bastions guarding a UNESCO old town.

taxi.fareNote: Campeche's street taxis are mostly unmetered, so agree the fare before setting off (short trips around the walled centre are cheap); Uber and DiDi operate with limited driver numbers but give an upfront price.

emergency.note: 911 is Mexico's unified emergency number for police, fire and ambulance; 078 is the national tourist assistance line.

hood_landmark.Centro Histórico (Ciudad Amurallada): the walled old town's Puerta de Tierra gate and pastel streets
hood_landmark.San Román: Iglesia de San Román, home of the revered Cristo Negro
hood_landmark.Barrio de Santa Ana: the Iglesia de Santa Ana and its traditional cocina económica eateries
hood_landmark.Guadalupe: Iglesia de Guadalupe, one of the peninsula's oldest churches
hood_landmark.San Francisco: Iglesia de San Francisco, among the earliest churches on the American mainland

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed walled old town of pastel colonial houses, cobbled streets, bastions (baluartes) and the land-and-sea gates; best for first-timers who want every sight, restaurant and the seafront Malecón within an easy walk.

A characterful barrio just outside the walls, predating the fortifications, centred on the church of San Román and its revered Black Christ; more lived-in and local than the restored centre, with good-value guesthouses.

One of Campeche's oldest barrios, spreading east of the walled city beyond the Puerta de Tierra around the Iglesia de Santa Ana; more lived-in than the restored centre, with everyday plazas, street food and cheap rooms a short walk from the walls.

A workaday residential barrio just north-east of the walls around the Iglesia de Guadalupe, an easy ten-minute walk from the historic core; practical and quieter, with mid-range hotels and everyday local life.

A historic district north of the centre where Hernández de Córdoba first landed, with colonial churches, street art and the hilltop fort of San José el Alto above; calmer and residential, a short ride from the walls.

water.note: Stick to bottled or purified water, as everywhere in Mexico.

transit.pay: Bus and colectivo fares are paid in cash to the driver (roughly MXN 8-12); there is no rechargeable transit card. Keep small change handy.
transit.hours: City buses and colectivos run roughly 5:30 AM to around 10:00 PM; taxis and ride apps fill the late-night gap.
transit.note: Campeche has no metro or rail transit; the compact walled Centro is best explored on foot, with city buses, colectivo combis and taxis covering the barrios and the Malecón. The panoramic 'Guagua' tram-bus runs tourist loops from the Plaza Principal.

landmarks: Centro Histórico and City Walls
A UNESCO-listed grid of candy-colored baroque facades enclosed by 17th-century ramparts, built after pirate raids and now Mexico's best-preserved fortified colonial town.
Fuerte de San Miguel
This hilltop fortress with drawbridge and moat houses the superb Museum of Maya Archaeology, displaying the jade funeral masks of Calakmul's ancient kings.
Catedral de Nuestra Señora de la Purísima Concepción
Twin limestone towers of this 16th-to-18th-century cathedral rise theatrically above the main plaza, glowing gold when floodlit against the tropical night sky.
Puerta de Tierra
The imposing 1732 Land Gate anchors the old walls, hosting an evening light-and-sound show that resurrects Campeche's swashbuckling pirate-siege history.
Calle 59
The walled city's prettiest street runs gate-to-gate past restored pastel townhouses, cafe terraces, and hanging lanterns, linking the Sea Gate with the Land Gate.
Malecón de Campeche
A palm-lined waterfront promenade curving several kilometers along the Gulf of Mexico, beloved for cycling, sculpture, and some of Mexico's most flamboyant sunsets.
Fuerte de San José el Alto
Perched on a breezy hill north of town, this 1792 fortress holds a museum of ships and arms with commanding views over the Gulf coastline.
Baluarte de Santiago and Xmuch'haltún Garden
A reconstructed corner bastion of the old walls sheltering a lush botanical garden of Yucatecan flora within its coral-stone courtyard.
Plaza de la Independencia (Parque Principal)
Campeche's graceful main square, ringed by arcaded portales, the cathedral, and a wrought-iron kiosk, comes alive with music and dancing on weekend evenings.
Baluarte de la Soledad (Museo de la Arquitectura Maya)
The largest bastion of Campeche's colonial sea wall, now home to a museum of Maya architectural fragments gathered from sites across the state.

train.note: No international trains, but the Tren Maya intercity railway stops at Campeche, linking the city with Mérida, Palenque and onward toward Cancún on the Yucatán Peninsula loop. It is one of the very few real passenger rail services in Mexico. Book on the official Tren Maya site; frequencies are still limited, so check the timetable before relying on it.

bus.note: No international coaches. ADO (https://www.ado.com.mx/) runs first-class services from the Campeche terminal frequently to Mérida (about 2h30), Ciudad del Carmen, Villahermosa, Palenque, Cancún and Mexico City (around 18 hours). Second-class buses to the Edzná ruins and nearby towns use a separate terminal.

ferry.note: Campeche sits on the Gulf but has no scheduled passenger ferry - the waterfront is a malecón promenade and the port handles minor cargo. The nearest passenger crossings are on the Caribbean coast to Cozumel and Isla Mujeres.

half.name: Playa Bonita & Lerma
half.blurb: The city's nearest Gulf beaches just south of town, a laid-back half-day of seafood palapas and warm shallow water.

full.name: Edzná Archaeological Zone
full.blurb: A monumental Maya city an hour inland, crowned by the five-storey Building of the Five Floors overlooking a great ceremonial plaza and an ingenious canal system.

full.name: Calakmul & the Biosphere Reserve
full.blurb: A vast Maya metropolis deep in the jungle near the Guatemalan border (a long full day), with towering pyramids rising above the rainforest canopy and abundant wildlife.

full.name: Isla Aguada & Laguna de Términos
full.blurb: A Gulf-coast lagoon town a couple of hours down the coast, where boat trips visit dolphin waters, mangroves and the long Isla del Carmen bridge.
